```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

# --- CONFIGURATION ---
# Set the name of the target distribution matching your simulation[cite: 4]
TARGET_DIST <- "exponential" 

# Adjust output directory path to match where your files were written[cite: 4]
data_dir <- "~/SJSU26F/MATH167R/CLT/data/exponential"

# Load saved simulation dataset and add necessary columns for tables[cite: 4]
summary_table <- read.csv(file.path(data_dir, "exp_metrics.csv")) %>%
  mutate(
    mean_bias = sim_mean - theo_mean,
    se_ratio = sim_se / theo_se
  )
```

## 1. Original Population Distribution

<!-- Question 1: What does the original population distribution look like? -->

- **Name / Class:** Exponential
- **Type:** Continuous, heavily right-skewed
- **Description:**
  <!-- Describe features: continuity, boundedness, symmetry/skewness, support, unimodal vs multimodal, etc. -->
  The exponential distribution is a distribution representing the
  occurrence of an event that will. happen on average once per unit of
  time. These events happen continuously and independently. An example
  used in class would be how late a professor is to class.

```{r}
#| label: fig-population-shape
#| fig-cap: "Theoretical / baseline shape of the population distribution (n = 1)."

ggplot() +
  xlim(0, 5) +
  stat_function(fun = dexp, args = list(rate=1), color = "#009E73", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Population Density:", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "x",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Theoretical Mean and Standard Deviation

- **Theoretical Mean (**$\mu$): 1\[cite: 4\]
- **Theoretical Standard Deviation (**$\sigma$): 1\[cite: 4\]

For an Exponential distribution $X \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$ with rate
parameter $\lambda = 1$, the PDF is:

$$f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}$$

The theoretical mean is calculated as:

$$\mu = \text{E}[X] = \frac{1}{\lambda} = 1$$

The theoretical standard deviation is derived from the variance:

$$\sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda^2}} = 1$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Rate of Convergence to Normality

<!-- Question 3: How quickly does the sampling distribution become approximately normal? --> 

- **Observations across sample sizes (**$n$):
  <!-- At what sample size n does skewness drop close to 0? Kurtosis near 0? --> Starting with a very high initial kurtosis score, it quickly approaches zero. Skewness also starts at a higher level and starts to converge rapidly. As this is a known distribution this is expected. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-shape-statistics
#| fig-cap: "Convergence of Skewness and Excess Kurtosis toward zero as sample size increases."

summary_table %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(skewness, excess_kurtosis), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = value, color = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("skewness" = "#009E73", "excess_kurtosis" = "orange")) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Shape Statistics vs. n for", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Metric Value",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```


------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Simulated Mean vs. Theoretical Mean

<!-- Question 4: How does the simulated mean compare with the theoretical mean? --> The simulated mean and theoretical mean show us if our Monte Carlo simulation model is behaving as expected.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mean-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated sample means vs. theoretical mean."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_mean, sim_mean, mean_bias) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical Mean (μ)", "Simulated Mean (X̄)", "Mean Bias (X̄ - μ)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:**
  <!-- Does the empirical mean stay close to the theoretical mean across all n? Is there any noticeable bias? --> The bias is very close to zero through the increases in sample size whihc says that the model is predicting correctly and there is not a large amount of bias in the simulation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Simulated Standard Error vs. Theoretical Standard Error

<!-- Question 5: How does the simulated standard error compare with SE(X̄) = σ / √n? -->

$$\text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-se-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated standard errors with theoretical SE = σ / √n."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_se, sim_se, se_ratio) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical SE", "Simulated SE", "SE Ratio (Sim / Theo)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:**
  <!-- Does the ratio sim_se / theo_se remain close to 1.0? Does the empirical spread decay at rate 1 / √n? --> The simulated standard error and theoretical standard error ratio is close to 1 though the increases in sample size which shows that the simulation is an ideal benchmark with low variability. 
  
------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Evidence for Normality

<!-- Question 6: What evidence supports your conclusion that the distribution is—or is not—approximately normal? -->

### Graphical Evidence (Density & Q-Q Plots)

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-dist-qq
#| fig-cap: "Standardized empirical density and Normal Q-Q plots across selected sample sizes $n$ ($B = 10{,}000$)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: "center"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(8676)

B <- 10000L
selected_n <- c(1, 20, 30, 35)

density_qq_list <- list()

for (n_val in selected_n) {
  observations <- rexp(B * n_val, rate = 1)
  sample_matrix <- matrix(observations, nrow = B, ncol = n_val)
  means <- rowMeans(sample_matrix)
  
  sim_mean <- mean(means)
  sim_se <- sd(means)
  
  z_means <- if (is.finite(sim_se) && sim_se > 0) (means - sim_mean) / sim_se else rep(NA_real_, B)
  density_qq_list[[length(density_qq_list) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    n_label = paste0("n = ", n_val),
    n_num = n_val,
    z = z_means
  )
}

plot_data <- bind_rows(density_qq_list) %>% filter(is.finite(z))
plot_data$n_label <- factor(plot_data$n_label, levels = paste0("n = ", selected_n))

tight_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 4, r = 6, b = 4, l = 6)
  )

p_dens_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = z)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.35, color = "#009E73", linewidth = 0.6) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Empirical Density vs N(0,1)", x = "Standardized Mean (Z)", y = "Density") +
  tight_theme

p_qq_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(sample = z)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray30") +
  stat_qq(color = "#009E73", alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plots", x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  tight_theme

p_dens_tight | p_qq_tight
```

- **Density Overlays:**
  <!-- Mention the alignment with the standard N(0, 1) curve. --> The density overlay charts show that due to the extreme right skewness of the exponential distribution, the sample mean distributions have a hard time shaking off the skewness that is left over. I think that by n = 30, the skewness settles down to an acceptable level. There is still some skewness but visually the n = 30 graph falls into the standard distribution well. 
- **Q-Q Plot Quantile Alignment:**
  <!-- Inspect the linearity in your Q-Q plots. --> The Q-Q plots approach linearity rather slowly. Interestingly the Q-Q plot for n = 35 appears less linear than 30 which is probably due to the randomness in the Monte Carlo simulation instead of something within the distribution. The linearity feels comfortable at the n = 30 mark although there is not much difference from n = 25. 

### Statistical Evidence (Shapiro-Wilk Test & Moment Ratios)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-normality-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Normality assessment metrics: Skewness, Kurtosis, and Shapiro-Wilk test."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, skewness, excess_kurtosis, shapiro_W, shapiro_p) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Skewness", "Excess Kurtosis", "Shapiro-Wilk W", "p-value")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Conclusion on Normality:**
  <!-- Summarize when the distribution meets practical and formal normality thresholds. --> According to the statistical tests, skewness and kurtosis do not approach 0 for some time, and at n = 30, are relatively high compared to other distributions. That being said, the W score for this distribution approaches 1 rather quickly meaning that it fits the normal distribution relatively well from n = 5 and beyond. 

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Limitations and Surprises

<!-- Question 7: What limitations or surprises did you observe? -->

- **Key Observations / Surprises:**
  <!-- e.g., persistent tail skewness, boundary effects, Shapiro-Wilk p-value sensitivity to large sample sizes, etc. --> There was a persistent skewness to the graph and I noticed across simulations there was not a very smooth graph peak until large sample sizes. 
- **Simulation Limitations:**
  <!-- e.g., finite Monte Carlo reps B = 10,000, fixed selection of n_values, truncation of sub-sample size for normality testing. --> I noticed the Monte Carlo simulation results affected the graph quite a bit resulting in high levels of visual variance between small sample size changes such as n = 30 and n = 31.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Final Verdict

#### Central Limit Theorem Confirmed at *n = 30*

<!-- Final thoughts on convergence --> I felt like the graphs tell the story here, the Shapiro Wilk W value approaches 1 fairly quickly and the main reasons for waiting until n = 30 were mostly due to the excess skewness that hung on throughout the graphs.
